title: Sockets, Ports & Encapsulation in a Live Client-Server Connection
topic: OSI/TCP-IP Models, Encapsulation, Interfaces, Client-Server Sockets
learning_objectives: Map POSIX socket API calls (socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, close) to TCP/IP and OSI layers.
Distinguish a server's listening socket file descriptor from an accepted client-connection socket file descriptor.
Trace how application payload bytes are encapsulated into TCP segments and IPv4 packets.
prerequisites: Basic C or Python programming familiarity

concept_explanation.title: OSI vs. TCP/IP Layering & Encapsulation
concept_explanation.summary: Networking stacks divide responsibilities into layers. Each layer wraps data from the layer above with its own header (encapsulation) on transmit and strips it (decapsulation) on receive.
key_points: Application data written via send() becomes TCP payload (Layer 4 Transport).
TCP adds source/destination ports, sequence/ack numbers, and flags; IPv4 (Layer 3 Network) adds source/destination IP addresses and TTL.
Link Layer (Layer 2) frames the packet for the local medium (Ethernet or loopback).

concept_explanation.title: Client-Server Socket Lifecycle & Ports
concept_explanation.summary: A server binds to a well-known local port (e.g., 127.0.0.1:8080) and listens, while the OS assigns the client an ephemeral source port during connect().
key_points: accept() returns a NEW file descriptor representing the specific client session; the original FD keeps listening.
Every TCP connection is uniquely identified by its 4-tuple: (client_ip, client_port, server_ip, server_port).

experiment.title: Observe a Live C POSIX TCP Echo Connection
experiment.instructions: Run the allowlisted POSIX C TCP echo server and client on loopback (127.0.0.1:8080). NetBox intercepts every POSIX socket call via LD_PRELOAD and simultaneously captures real IPv4/TCP packets via libpcap.
required_setup: Optional: netbox_pcap with cap_net_raw for wire-level packet capture
execution_steps: Select the 'Complete TCP Echo (Foundations)' scenario and click Run Experiment.
Open the 'Overview & Socket API' tab and step through socket -> bind -> listen -> connect -> accept -> send -> recv -> close.
Switch to the 'Packets' and 'Correlations' tabs to map application send()/recv() calls to IPv4/TCP wire segments.

supported_scenarios.label: Complete TCP Echo (Foundations)
supported_scenarios.description: Runs the C TCP echo server and client on 127.0.0.1:8080 with full socket + packet capture.

expected_observations: Server performs socket() -> bind(127.0.0.1:8080) -> listen() before client calls connect().
accept() returns a new socket FD distinct from the listening FD.
Client uses an OS-assigned ephemeral source port while server listens on port 8080.
Real captured IPv4+TCP packets show encapsulation: link header + 20B IPv4 header + TCP header + payload.
observation_caveats: User-space socket_api events and wire-level packet_capture events are distinct layers — kernel ACKs appear as packets without separate application send() calls.

questions.prompt: In the server process trace, why does accept() return a different file descriptor number than the one returned by socket()?
options: Because the kernel closes the listening socket as soon as one client connects.
Because the listening socket stays open to accept future connections while the new FD represents this specific client's 4-tuple session.
Because POSIX requires every TCP packet to allocate a fresh file descriptor.
Because accept() runs inside the client process rather than the server process.
questions.rubric_summary: Listening FD stays open for new connections; accepted FD tracks the established 4-tuple session.
questions.explanation: accept() allocates a new connected socket FD for the established client session so the original listening FD can continue queuing incoming connections.

questions.prompt: If the client sends a 22-byte message over IPv4 TCP (20-byte IP header, 32-byte TCP header with timestamps), what IPv4 total_length do you expect in the captured packet?
questions.rubric_summary: IPv4 total_length = IP header (20) + TCP header (32) + payload (22) = 74 bytes.
questions.explanation: Encapsulation adds the Layer 3 header (20 B) and Layer 4 TCP header (32 B) to the 22 B payload, yielding an IPv4 total_length of 74 bytes.

questions.prompt: Briefly explain why a captured trace can show more TCP packets than application send() calls.
questions.rubric_summary: Mention kernel-generated control segments (SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK, FIN) that occur without explicit send() calls.
questions.explanation: The OS TCP stack generates control segments (SYN, SYN+ACK, pure ACKs, FINs) automatically in response to connect(), accept(), recv(), and close() without separate application send() calls.

completion_criteria.description: Execute the Foundations TCP echo experiment and score at least 67% on the assessment.
